sense.text: “He made the moon also to serve in her season for a declaration of times, and a sign of the world.” The moon was made to serve: she declares the times and the seasons.

“From the moon is the sign of feasts, a light that decreaseth in her perfection.” The moon is the sign of the feasts. She starts off full and then begins to decrease, so she is in her perfection, her completion, when she is full.

That light in her perfection, the full moon, is the designator for when the feast days are to be kept.

“The month is called after her name”: the word month comes from moon. “Increasing wonderfully in her changing”: she goes from decreasing back to increasing until she is perfect again.

“Being an instrument of the armies above”: the armies above are the angels. “Shining in the firmament of heaven”, shining in the sky.

“The beauty of heaven, the glory of the stars, an ornament giving light in the highest places of the Lord.” Giving light: not dark and unseen, not a sliver of light. Giving light is her perfection.

Read Ecclesiasticus 43 from verse 1 on down and it speaks of the rainbow, the sun and the moon, all the ornaments of heaven when they are bright and at their highest, at their peak: not at dusk, not at sundown. Every one of them is spoken of in its glory, in its perfection. So the moon in her glory, which is full, is the sign of the feast. Not the moon unseen, when no one knows where it is.

precepts.why:
“And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years”. For signs: signs of the times, signs of the world, as Ecclesiasticus says the moon is “a sign of the world.” And for seasons: to determine the feast days that fall in their seasons.

“And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day”, that is the sun, “and the lesser light to rule the night”, that is the moon. “He made the stars also”: the stars and the planets, the same thing. “And God set them in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth.”

So from the very beginning the moon was set in the heaven for the seasons, and the feasts of the Lord are kept by her.

“This month shall be unto you the beginning of months: it shall be the first month of the year to you.” That is the new moon. The first thing given to us was our new moon, because under Egypt they had a ten-day week, so the Lord had to let us know: this is the time when your month begins.

The month is called after the moon, and the moon begins the months of Israel’s year.
“This day came ye out in the month Abib.” That first month of the year to us is Abib, late March to early April. Not January, not February: that is not the new year. In Babylon it was called Nisan.

sense.text:
“Concerning the feasts of the Lord”: feasts, more than one, “which ye shall proclaim to be holy convocations”. Holy convocations are holy gatherings, where you assemble yourselves together. To convoke means to come together: holy convocations are assemblies. How individuals keep it on their own is hard to see when it says holy convocations.

“Even these are my feasts.” Verse 2 is the introduction to the feast days as a whole.

“The seventh day is the sabbath of rest, an holy convocation”. The Sabbath is a weekly feast, and it too is a holy convocation, a holy assembly, a gathering. “Ye shall do no work therein”.

“It is the sabbath of the Lord in all your dwellings”: wherever you dwell, regardless of where you are, in the land or outside the land, that is your Sabbath.

A new paragraph. Verse 2 is the feast days as a whole, verse 3 is the seventh day Sabbath, and now verse 4 is something else: “These are the feasts of the Lord, even holy convocations”. Convocations, plural, more than one. Verse 3 said convocation, the Sabbath; these are assemblies beyond the one Sabbath.

“Which ye shall proclaim in their seasons.” These are the seasonal feasts: Passover in verse 5 in the spring, the first fruits, and so on into the fall. And what is used to determine the seasonal feast days? The moon, the full moon in her perfection.

“In the seventh month, in the first day of the month, shall ye have a sabbath, a memorial of blowing of trumpets, an holy convocation.” We kept this one recently.

This new moon is a Sabbath, but it is not the same as the seventh day Sabbath. The new moon Sabbath and the seventh day Sabbath are two distinct Sabbaths: one monthly, and one weekly, which runs irrespective of the days of the months.

“Also on the tenth day of this seventh month there shall be a day of atonement”. The first day of the seventh month is the new moon, the blowing of trumpets; the tenth day of it is the Day of Atonement. “It shall be an holy convocation unto you”.

“And ye shall afflict your souls”: that is not clarified here. Moses does not say what it means, so we have to go somewhere else to explain it.

“And offer an offering made by fire unto the Lord”: a sacrifice on that day. So during Mosaic times, on the Day of Atonement, we had to afflict our souls and then offer up sacrifices. Keep that in mind. It is very important.

“And ye shall do no work in that same day”, because it is a Sabbath, “for it is a day of atonement, to make an atonement for you before the Lord your God.”

“Whatsoever soul it be that shall not be afflicted in that same day, he shall be cut off from among his people”: be killed. “Whatsoever soul it be that doeth any work in that same day, the same soul will I destroy from among his people.” Cut off and destroy are synonymous: the end of verse 29 and the end of verse 30 say the same thing. Both mean to kill.

“It shall be a statute for ever throughout your generations in all your dwellings.” Like the weekly Sabbath, wherever you are in this world, whether in Jerusalem or outside Jerusalem, it is a statute throughout all your generations. Are we still generating? Yes. So we are still to keep it.

“It shall be unto you a sabbath of rest”. That is why no work shall be done therein, or you will be cut off, killed, destroyed. The commandment to keep the Sabbath day holy is not about one Sabbath only: there are multiple Sabbaths, depending on the feast day, and the Day of Atonement falls under it as well.

“In the ninth day of the month at even”: the ninth day at evening is the tenth day. “From even unto even, shall ye celebrate your sabbath.” From evening to evening, not day to day. That is how we counted our days: when the sun went down and it was dark outside, from dark to dark. The day begins at night and it ends at night.

Those who believed in a sunrise Sabbath, where are they today? Gone with the wind, out in the world eating chicken and pork.

precepts.why:
“In the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, ye shall afflict your souls, and do no work at all, whether it be one of your own country, or a stranger that sojourneth among you”.

“For on that day shall the priest make an atonement for you, to cleanse you, that ye may be clean from all your sins before the Lord.” Shall the priest: remember, on that day you offered sacrifices, and it was the priest who made the atonement. “The priest, whom he shall anoint, and whom he shall consecrate to minister in the priest’s office in his father’s stead, shall make the atonement, and shall put on the linen clothes, even the holy garments”. He made an atonement for the holy sanctuary, for the tabernacle of the congregation, for the altar, for the priests, “and for all the people of the congregation.”

“And this shall be an everlasting statute unto you, to make an atonement for the children of Israel for all their sins once a year.” For all their sins, once a year. The Day of Atonement is done once a year: a statute forever, to make an atonement for all our sins.

“And Aaron shall make an atonement upon the horns of it once in a year with the blood of the sin offering of atonements”. Once in a year, and with blood: the blood of the sin offering of atonement. “Once in the year shall he make atonement upon it throughout your generations: it is most holy unto the Lord.”

So the offering made by fire on the Day of Atonement was the blood of the sin offering, once a year.

sense.text:
Isaiah 58 explains what it means to afflict your souls. Not hitting yourself in the face.

“Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not? wherefore have we afflicted our soul”: so fasting and afflicting your soul are the same thing. The prophets explain what Moses does not: afflicting your soul means to fast.

“And thou takest no knowledge?” Israel complained: we are fasting, we are praying, and the Most High is not listening to us. “Behold, in the day of your fast ye find pleasure, and exact all your labours”: they did their own business, they worked, they made their money, when the scripture says specifically that it is a Sabbath, no work. Israel did what they wanted to do in this time, so the Most High was not listening to them at all.

“Behold, ye fast for strife and debate, and to smite with the fist of wickedness”. They fasted and fought among themselves, debate going around like a virus, back and forth, getting into confrontations.

“Ye shall not fast as ye do this day, to make your voice to be heard on high.” You are going to fast, but you cannot do it the way you have been doing it: fighting among yourselves, working, arguing, debating. That fast is a waste of time; the Most High is not listening to that.
“Is it such a fast that I have chosen? a day for a man to afflict his soul?” To afflict his soul is to fast.

“Is not this the fast that I have chosen?” We have many fasts, but the scripture says the fast: that is the Day of Atonement.

“To loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens”: that is to cleanse you of all your sins. That is what he is talking about.

“Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house?” Look out for each other: love your neighbour as yourself.

“That thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh”: your own people. We were not doing that. We were doing all kinds of evil, and fasting anyway.

“Then shall thy light break forth as the morning”: when you stop doing those things, then I will listen to you. “Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer; thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I am.”

But it is “If thou take away from the midst of thee the yoke, the putting forth of the finger, and speaking vanity”: the debating, the arguing, the confrontations.

“And if thou draw out thy soul to the hungry”: look out for your people who are poor. “And satisfy the afflicted soul”: feed them. “Then shall thy light rise in obscurity”, out of darkness, “and thy darkness be as the noonday”: you will be in the light.

“And the Lord shall guide thee continually, and satisfy thy soul in drought, and make fat thy bones”: the Most High will look out for you. “Thou shalt be like a watered garden”: with understanding, nourished.

“And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations”. That is to return to our land again: it is a prophecy. “And thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in”, if we do these things right.

“If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath”: the sabbath here is the fast of verse 6, the Day of Atonement. “From doing thy pleasure on my holy day”: the pleasure back in verse 3, which is business, making money, labouring, fighting, arguing, debating. That was their pleasure: doing what they wanted against his laws, on his holy day, the fast.

“And call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the Lord, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words”. Doing what you want to do, fasting how you want to fast. I’ll have a water fast, I’ll have a juice fast: no. Fasting means nothing: no eating, no drinking, nothing at all.

precepts.why:
This is what fasting is. “The people of Nineveh believed God, and proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them even to the least of them.”

“And he caused it to be proclaimed and published through Nineveh by the decree of the king and his nobles, saying, Let neither man nor beast, herd nor flock, taste any thing: let them not feed, nor drink water”. Taste nothing. No eating, no drinking, nothing at all: twenty-four hours of no eating nor drinking, evening to evening. You are not going to die. Once a year, you will be just fine.

Taste nothing means no brushing of the teeth. No trying to be slick, opening your mouth in the shower. No putting Vaseline on and licking your lips on purpose. Do not eat, do not drink anything.

Isaiah 58 mentions the fast. Did Paul keep it? Christianity says it was done away with in the New Testament. “Now when much time was spent, and when sailing was now dangerous, because the fast was now already past, Paul admonished them”.

Verse 6: “And there the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing into Italy; and he put us therein.” Alexandria is in Egypt, and the ship was sailing to Italy, to Rome. So Paul kept the fast on a boat, on the Day of Atonement. He was not in Jerusalem; he was sailing, travelling, in this time.

The fast was on the tenth day of the seventh month, Leviticus 23:27-29: the Day of Atonement, which Isaiah 58 calls the fast. In Moses’ time the priest offered sacrifices for us on it once a year. But once Christ died on the cross, Paul could keep it without the sacrificing, because Christ was that sacrifice.

sense.text: “Therefore also now, saith the Lord, turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning”. Turn with fasting, with weeping, with mourning: repentance, with a sincere heart and sincere remorse.

“And rend your heart, and not your garments”. Christianity has its own reading of this, but what it means is this: in Israel, whenever we went into an affliction or a sadness, we rent, we ripped our clothes. The Lord says rend your mind: repent.

Ripping your clothes does not mean a damn thing to him. You are wicked as hell, and you rip your clothes because you feel bad. No: you have to fast, and be sincere about it.

“And turn unto the Lord your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil.” With fasting, with weeping, with mourning: rend your heart.

“He that covereth his sins shall not prosper”. The atonement is a time of self-reflection. Once a year you examine your sins, what you have done. Some are battling hatred, anger, fornication, jealousy, envy, whatever it may be. Bitterness: that is a big one in here.

You cannot hide those things. Over time they leak out of you and corrupt you. There are three Fs: it festers, it ferments, and it becomes fragmented.

Fester: for a negative feeling or a bad situation to grow worse over time because it is ignored. When those spirits are on you, it grows, it spreads, it gets worse and worse, and you refuse to acknowledge it. You ignore it and leave it alone. That is what happens with bitterness, anger, hatred, sadness, and depression too.

Ferment: to undergo a change, to be in a state of agitation; turmoil, unrest, commotion, upheaval; it brews, it seethes, it boils. First it festers in you for a long time; then it ferments and begins to change you. Your behaviour starts to change and it shows. You cannot remain that way for years without it becoming visible: you see it in the face, the black under the eyes, the countenance changes. They act different, they speak different, they isolate themselves and spend less time around the brothers and sisters.

At first: brother, you all right? Yeah, I’m good. You sure? I’m fine. Meanwhile they are mad. Then it brews, and Satan starts playing in your head: that nigga is the devil, he hates your guts. Everyone is wicked but you. You are the most holy, you know all the scriptures, you are the wisest in the room. When it ferments, you and Satan are best friends. You are driving and he is in the passenger seat, and then he says, I’ll take it from here, take a nap, and destroys every damn thing. Some even say, I’m not the same person. Really? I wonder who that could be. The Lord is not there.

It festers one year, two years, three years; then it is under fermentation and you begin to devolve, to degenerate. Everybody becomes the bad guy: I’m holy, I’ll stay to myself and pray, only y’all are evil, only I see the spirit. Satan says, you’re right, brother, you’re so deep, your Bible turns its own pages, you float across the room, you should sit on the panel, you should be an officer of two billion.

“But whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.” If you have a problem, speak on it: I have an issue, I have a problem. If you will not speak on it, it festers and it ferments, and then comes the third step: fragmentation. Fragmentation is the process of breaking something into smaller separate pieces. A fragment is a small piece that has broken off, separated from a whole: a part broken off, detached, incomplete.

precepts.why:
This is what fragmentation is. “These be they who separate themselves, sensual, having not the Spirit.” They separate themselves: that is the fragment, broken off from the whole. Sensual: emotional, sinful. Having not the Spirit.

“But ye, beloved, building up yourselves on your most holy faith”. You have to build yourself. No one can be in your brain to tell you what to do. You know what is in you; you know if you are angry, bitter, hateful, sad or depressed. That is on you, and you have to speak on it. Some do and some do not, and those who do not grow worse and worse over time.

They separate themselves: now they are in the back of the school, the back of the class. Everyone is gathered at a table with the leadership, and they leave. Shalom, y’all. You got work tomorrow? Nah, I got things to do. That is fragmentation. Fester, ferment, fragment: the three Fs. It is like the herd on the nature channel and that one ox that wanders off by itself.

Peter says the same thing as Jude, that they separate themselves, having not the spirit: “But chiefly them that walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness, and despise government. Presumptuous are they, selfwilled, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities.”

That is the fragmentation. Over time you become a Judas. You become untrustworthy, and everyone becomes the enemy. Now you are doing videos on why you left; it is downhill from there. Now you are eating chicken nuggets on Passover.

From festering, to fermentation, to fragmentation: there are steps to it, over time.

“Instead of a friend become not an enemy; for thereby thou shalt inherit an ill name, shame, and reproach”. That is the fragmentation, what happens over time when you let it fester and ferment, seethe and boil. You become untrustworthy; you act beside yourself. Now you inherit an ill name: we want to bring so-and-so along with us? Nah, he can stay back. Want her to work in the kitchen? Nah, she is acting kind of weird; let her sit down with her kids over there.

“Even so shall a sinner that hath a double tongue.” In one breath: bless, brother, how you doing? In the back of your mind: I can’t stand him, I hate her guts. That is double minded, double tongued, talking out of both sides of your neck, because of the festering, the fermenting and the fragmentation.

“Extol not thyself in the counsel of thine own heart”. Verse 2 is what took place for verse 1 to happen, for you to become the enemy in the first place: you took counsel from your own mind, your own thoughts and feelings. Sensual: emotional. “That thy soul be not torn in pieces as a bull straying alone.” What happens to a bull straying alone? He is torn to pieces by the lion, and who is the lion in the Bible? The devil. The one that wanders off from the herd to drink by himself, the lion creeps up, bites him in the back and drags him down. It is a wrap; he is food, because he strayed from the herd. Do not stray from the herd. Do not fragment.

Many brothers and sisters do just that: mad, angry, thinking they are wiser than anybody in the room, and no one can tell them anything. Some for months, some for years, until they turn into a mad man or a mad woman, bugged out in the world. You will not last in here like that.

“Thou shalt eat up thy leaves, and lose thy fruit, and leave thyself as a dry tree.” Over time you lose your understanding: whatever you think you know, you will forget.

“A wicked soul shall destroy him that hath it, and shall make him to be laughed to scorn of his enemies.” Instead of a friend you became an enemy and strayed alone, and now you are laughed at by those who were once your friends. Remember that dude who used to be with us, the captain of so-and-so? Sunrise Sabbath. Where is he now? Now you are a joke, a story to tell, a character, because you turned against the brothers who looked out for you and your family. Lost in the wind.

“Sweet language will multiply friends”. “Be in peace with many: nevertheless have but one counsellor of a thousand.” If you are going through something, you do not have to tell the whole world, but talk to someone: one counsellor. And if you say, I talk to the Bible, I talk to the laws: no, brother; no, sister. That is extolling yourself in your own mind, verse 2. It sounds good, but the scripture says one counsellor among a thousand. “If thou wouldest get a friend, prove him first, and be not hasty to credit him”: that is the one counsellor.

“Separate thyself from thine enemies, and take heed of thy friends.” When you see a brother doing verses 1 through 4, keep him at arm’s length. We see it festering, we see it fermenting, we see the fragmentation. And take heed of your friends: be very mindful how they act, because they might become verses 1 through 4 through the bitterness that is in them.

sense.text:
“Wherefore laying aside all malice”. We read these words all the time and gloss over them. Malice is the intention or desire to cause harm, pain or distress to another person. It is internal. Some people feel good doing it; they have joy in hurting people, in animosity and hatred toward people. The road to hell is paved with good intentions. It is not a good place to be.

Even certain Israelite camps have that same spirit, looking for evil, looking for a way to destroy and discredit us. We have done nothing to you at all. You guys are gay. How do you know? You don’t know me. That is malice. It takes time to build that, sitting there despising people you do not even know. It is an evil spirit to have.

Malicious: spiteful, malevolent, vicious. Malevolent: having or showing a strong, lasting wish to do evil or cause harm to others. That strong lasting wish is the ferment; that is a demon in you, an evil spirit. Malignant: tending to produce death or severe harm, which goes back to the fermentation. Vindictive: a strong desire for revenge, which goes into the fragmentation, straying alone, separating yourself: I ain’t coming to the school that day, I’ll stay home and watch online, because I can’t stand them. Some have that spirit, and it stands out.

In close-knit circles and congregations (the Bishop speaks all the time about having a circle you can trust), when a brother acts weird it is noticeable. He is going through something, and rather than say something he keeps it to himself, and over time he shows resentment toward other people. You see it.

“And all guile”: deception. “And hypocrisies, and envies”: envy is secret hatred. “And all evil speakings”. You have to lay these things aside.

“As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby”. You grow when you lay aside the malice, the guile, the hypocrisies, the envies and the evil speakings, and only then.

Otherwise you are spiritually stillborn, just sitting here taking up space. Once brothers and sisters, now sitting there while class is going on, no notes taken, just looking around mad, full of hate. Happy Sabbath, malignant and malevolent. Or you will grow, but the wrong way: to the left hand side of the Lord, not the right.

precepts.why:
Paul says the same thing as Peter: “Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice”. Bitterness is the first word he mentions. Clamour is murmuring. And all of it ties back to malice.

It is the same thing as Isaiah 58: the putting forth of the finger, the smiting with the fist of wickedness, finding your own pleasure. Some brothers take pleasure in malice and hatred; that is their pleasure too.

It also turns into Sabbath sickness: showing up for the feast days and the outings outside of school, but on the Sabbath, I’m sick, I don’t feel good. Why? Because there is festering, fermentation or fragmentation going on in there. Maybe it is your wife in your ear: so-and-so doesn’t like you, he hates your guts. Wormtongue in your ear, like Lord of the Rings, telling you all kinds of evil.

Some have cliques in here. Cliques are to be despised and avoided at all costs, because then a brother with an evil spirit feels comfortable coming to you with evil about somebody else. Why is he coming to you about that? Go talk to him. And examine yourself: why is the brother who has hatred toward him coming to you? It might mean something is in you also. Why are Korah, Dathan and Abiram approaching you? That is the spirit of Korah: hatred.

“And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another”, which is very hard for some people, “even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you.”

sense.text:
“But unto them that repent, he granted them return”. “Return unto the Lord, and forsake thy sins, make thy prayer before his face, and offend less.”

Offend less, because you are going to make mistakes. You may say something out of turn or disrespectful, not meant from the heart. You are going to fall, trip, and slip down the road. But offend less, as much as you can.
“Turn again to the most High, and turn away from iniquity: for he will lead thee out of darkness into the light of health, and hate thou abomination vehemently.”

“Who shall praise the most High in the grave, instead of them which live and give thanks?” Some will keep that hatred until they die. You cannot repent in the grave. Once you are dead and gone, there is no, I’m sorry, I forgive you now. That is over.

You have time in your life to fix things. If you have a problem with a brother or a sister, fix it now while you are still here; no one can determine what tomorrow will bring. Bring it to their attention. Some choose the Day of Atonement to do that, but you should have done it way before.

“Thanksgiving perisheth from the dead, as from one that is not: the living and sound in heart shall praise the Lord.”

“When one buildeth, and another pulleth down, what profit have they then but labour? When one prayeth, and another curseth, whose voice will the Lord hear?” If one is praying for you and one brother is cursing, whose voice will the Lord hear?

“He that washeth himself after the touching of a dead body, if he touch it again, what availeth his washing? So is it with a man that fasteth for his sins, and goeth again, and doeth the same”: he fasts for his sins, or she fasts for hers, and still has hatred in the heart, still bitterness.

“Who will hear his prayer? or what doth his humbling profit him?” Nothing. If you are out here fasting with bitterness in your heart, hatred, anger, malevolence, you are wasting your day and starving yourself for no reason. With that festering, fermenting, fragmenting spirit, just eat: have a graham cracker, have some grape juice, some Kool-Aid, some purple drink.

“He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.” When you keep the commandments of God, that is sacrifice enough. Sacrificing was a temporary thing.

“To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to the Lord; and to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation.” Propitiation goes back to atonement: conciliation to the Lord, bringing you close to the Lord.

“Diminish not the firstfruits of thine hands”: sacrifice. “In all thy gifts shew a cheerful countenance, and dedicate thy tithes with gladness.”

Do not walk around depressed and angry and sad. That spirit is contagious. Some walk around with a miserable countenance, sad all the time, woe is me. Some sit in the audience and look up on purpose to get attention: look at me, look at my tears. We ignore that.

“Do not think to corrupt with gifts; for such he will not receive”. That goes into bribery: having hatred for your brother, but offering the best sacrifice so the Most High will overlook it. I will offer the best of my flock, but I can’t stand that brother across the street. The Most High does not care about that: it is a corrupt gift, and he will not receive it.

“And trust not to unrighteous sacrifices; for the Lord is judge, and with him is no respect of persons.” He does not care about your best ox or your best sheep. If you have hatred for your people or your brother, it is a waste of a sacrifice and a waste of time.

precepts.why:
Christ says the same thing. “But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment”. Without a cause: sometimes a brother will make you angry, but this is without a cause. “Whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca”, you are a fool, “shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.” Because he will maintain that anger, that rage, that wrath against you forever.

Matthew 5:22 is bitterness. Whatever you say to them, they do not care. You try an intervention: brother, you all right? I’m good. No, you are not good. At some point they will destroy themselves, or be destroyed. Sisters the same.

“Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee”: in offering that sacrifice you remember your brother has an issue with you, or you with him, unresolved. “Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother”: fix things with your brother or sister first, “and then come and offer thy gift.”

Otherwise it becomes a corrupt, unrighteous gift, as Ecclesiasticus says. If you have not reconciled with your brother or sister, the gift is useless. It is not sincere. It is a lie.

sense.text: “Then verily the first covenant had also ordinances of divine service”: the first covenant is temple law. “And a worldly sanctuary”: a building on the earth, a temple. “For there was a tabernacle made; the first, wherein was the candlestick, and the table, and the shewbread; which is called the sanctuary”, or the temple.

“The priests went always into the first tabernacle, accomplishing the service of God. But into the second went the high priest alone”. The second part of the temple is the holy of holies, the holiest portion of the temple, and only the high priest was allowed to enter it.

“Once every year”: that is the atonement of Leviticus 16 and Exodus 30:10, once every year. “Not without blood”: the blood of sin offerings. “Which he offered for himself”, for his own sins, because these high priests were sinful too, “and for the errors of the people”.

Under the first testament the sin offering was done with blood. That is why it says not without blood: sacrifice was always done in those times, and especially once a year for the sins of all the people.

“The Holy Ghost this signifying, that the way into the holiest of all was not yet made manifest, while as the first tabernacle was yet standing”. The way into the holy of holies, by that sacrifice, was not made manifest yet.

“Which was a figure for the time then present, in which were offered both gifts and sacrifices, that could not make him that did the service perfect, as pertaining to the conscience”. The sacrificing of Aaron and his sons did not make them perfect. Offering animals did not make a person perfect, because they were still sinful, so the sacrifices were done daily and once a year: they were sinful all the time. As pertaining to the conscience, the mind, because sin is in our minds all the time.

“Which stood only in meats and drinks”: meat offerings and drink offerings, “and divers washings, and carnal ordinances, imposed on them until the time of reformation.” The reformation is when Christ set foot on the scene and brought the reform of no longer needing sacrifices.

Verse 11 explains the reformation: “But Christ being come an high priest of good things to come, by a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is to say, not of this building”: not the temple that stood on the ground, on earth.

“Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us.” Verse 7 said once every year; now it is once. When Christ died on the cross, he entered into the holy place in the heavens. The tabernacle, which was a tent in Moses’ time, and the building Solomon built on David’s blueprint, were a model, a figure, of the temple in the heavens that Christ entered for us one time, to be our atonement once and for all. By his own blood he removed the blood of goats and calves: that sacrificing is done away with.

“For if the blood of bulls and of goats, and the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh”. The ashes of an heifer were a cleansing agent, like a bleach, put in the water to purify the people. Sprinkling the unclean: baptisms.

“How much more shall the blood of Christ”: Christ’s blood is what that purifying water represents. Rather than using the ashes of an heifer to purify us, Christ dying on the cross purified us forever. “Who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God”, the faultless sacrifice, shall “purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God”.

“And almost all things are by the law purged with blood”: by the law of sacrifice, the blood of animals. That is the law Paul references all the time in his letters as being done away with.

Why almost all things? Because under the old covenant certain sins could not be purged. Homosexuality: off with your head. Breaking the Sabbath: off with your head. Choosing not to purify yourself after being unclean: off with your head. Witchcraft: off with your head. No atonement for that, no animal for you, no scapegoat for you: just death.

“And without shedding of blood is no remission”: without the blood of animals there was no forgiveness, no atonement, no justification.

“It was therefore necessary that the patterns of things in the heavens”, the temple, “should be purified with these”, with animals; “but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these.” That is Christ.

“For Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of the true”: the holy of holies on earth was a figure, a symbol, of the true temple in the heavens. “But into heaven itself”, into the real temple that the temple on earth is modeled after, “now to appear in the presence of God for us.” He presented himself to the Father on our behalf, and he is our advocate, our reconciliation, our eternal atonement.

“Nor yet that he should offer himself often, as the high priest entereth into the holy place every year with blood of others”: Christ does not have to do that. “For then must he often have suffered since the foundation of the world”: he would have had to die over and over again.

“But now once in the end of the world”, in the last days, “hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.” By the sacrifice of himself, atoning for us.

precepts.why:
“And for an unclean person they shall take of the ashes of the burnt heifer of purification for sin, and running water shall be put thereto in a vessel”. Purification for sin. You put the ashes of the heifer in the water and it becomes like a soap, a cleaning agent: ashes is soap, that is how you make soap. The running water is called living waters, and those waters were symbolic of Christ.

It was put in a vessel, the laver, to wash the person: that is baptism. Baptism was not John’s creation. John was of the priest line, of the Levites, and he was doing the same thing in the wilderness, dipping the people in water to purify them.

“And a clean person shall take hyssop, and dip it in the water, and sprinkle it upon the tent, and upon all the vessels, and upon the persons that were there, and upon him that touched a bone, or one slain, or one dead, or a grave”: that is the unclean. “And on the seventh day he shall purify himself, and wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water, and shall be clean at even.” In the water with the heifer: that is what it was for. So it was not just water we were cleansed with; it was soap also.

“But the man that shall be unclean, and shall not purify himself, that soul shall be cut off from among the congregation”: if a man was unclean and did not wash himself, he was killed for it, “because he hath defiled the sanctuary of the Lord: the water of separation hath not been sprinkled upon him; he is unclean.”

With that context, Hebrews 9:13: the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean was that washing, and the blood of Christ is what purifies us now.

sense.text: “For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect.” The same as Hebrews 9:9: those sacrifices could not make him that did the service perfect.

“For then would they not have ceased to be offered? because that the worshippers once purged should have had no more conscience of sins.” If sacrifice made you perfect, you would not have to offer it again and again. It was temporary.

“But in those sacrifices”, the law spoken of in verse 1, the meat offerings, drink offerings, purifications, temple law, “there is a remembrance again made of sins every year”: every year, the atonement.

“For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins.” “Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not”: the Most High had no care for sacrificing. It was a schoolmaster, a stepping stone leading us to Christ, a practice run to see how we would do before Christ showed up. What he cared about was obedience. Samuel and Judith say the same: the Most High does not care about sacrifices, he cares about obedience.

“But a body hast thou prepared”: that is Christ’s body. “In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin thou hast had no pleasure. Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God.”
“By the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all”: when he entered into the temple in the heavens.

“And every priest standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins”. Daily, every day. The Day of Atonement was year by year, and sacrifices were offered every day, because Israel was sinful every day.

“But this man”, Christ, “after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever”, himself, “sat down on the right hand of God”. He did not stand in the corner; he is not sitting on the Father’s kneecap or his shoulders. He sat down in his own seat on the right hand of God: two thrones, not one.

“From henceforth expecting till his enemies be made his footstool.” He is sitting there expecting, waiting, so it is time to take us home and get us out of here. Come on, keep the commandments, so I can come down there, kill people and get you out of there. He is sitting there tapping his feet: y’all keep messing up.

“For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.” Perfected: completed. We believe in Christ, so we are no longer required to offer up animals. We keep the feast days, but no longer with the sacrificing of animals. We keep the Day of Atonement, but we do not need to offer an animal any more, because Christ did away with that.

Christianity says Christ did away with thou shalt not kill and thou shalt not steal. How insane that sounds: steal all you want, lie all you want, rape and kill and pillage, just have your heart in Christ, and he will forgive you; believe while you steal and lie and fornicate. That is the church. The Christian church is garbage.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners”, in sin and darkness, “Christ died for us.”

“Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him.” We are justified by his blood. Under the Mosaic law we were justified by the blood of animals, animal sacrifice. Justify, atone and reconcile are the same word. Saved from wrath: saved from death through him.

“For if, when we were enemies”, God’s enemies, “we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son”: reconciled, justified, atoned for. “Much more, being reconciled”: being brought back to the Father again. Only we are reconciled to God, because to be reconciled means you were with God before. What other nation was with God before? None. How are they going to reconcile with God? They can’t.

“We shall be saved by his life.” We were saved by his death, and we are saved by his life.

“And not only so, but we also joy in God through our Lord Jesus Christ”: we serve our God with joyfulness and gladness in Christ now, no longer sacrificing animals. “By whom we have now received the atonement.” The margin gives reconciliation.

So atonement is reconciliation; atonement is justification. Christ justified us, atoned for us, and reconciled us back to his Father. Animals are no longer needed, but we still keep the feast days, including the Day of Atonement.

precepts.why:
How do we joy in God, and how do we serve him? “Because thou servedst not the Lord thy God with joyfulness, and with gladness of heart, for the abundance of all things”.

We did not serve our God with joyfulness and gladness in the feast days and the commandments. We would fast and do evil, keep the Sabbath and do evil, keep Tabernacles and do evil, keep Passover and do evil. The Lord said, you did not keep my commandments in joy and gladness, and for that reason I am going to put you in slavery.

Now, in Christ, we joy in God and serve him with gladness, no longer with the sacrificing of animals.

sense.text:
“Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you”. Springing up: that is the ferment. “And thereby many be defiled”.

Bitterness is an uncleanness, a defilement. Hatred, envy, wrath and malice are a defilement. You are unclean when you walk around like that, no matter how much you fast.

precepts.why:
“Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is”: the manner, the behaviour, of those who let their anger, bitterness and hatred fester, ferment and fragment over time, the sensual who separate themselves. That is why Leviticus 23 said these are holy convocations, holy assemblies. When you are bitter you are separating yourself slowly; you are defiled over time, a spot.

“But exhorting one another”, encouraging one another, “and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching”: so much more being around each other. Why? So we can go home and get out of here. Aren’t you tired of being here? Don’t you want to see this place burn? I love nukes: I would get a job at a nuclear factory and shine the nuclear bombs with a napkin every day. Shout out to Oppenheimer, Niels Bohr, Jack Parsons and Einstein: praise the Lord that he moved men to make bombs, so we can get out of here.

sense.text: “And these things write we unto you, that your joy may be full.” Your joy: the joy spoken of earlier in Romans 5:11, the joy we have in God through Christ.
“This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.”

“If we say that we have fellowship with him”: convocation, assembling ourselves together with him, “and walk in darkness”: with hatred and bitterness in our hearts and minds, “we lie”: we are lying to ourselves, nobody else, “and do not the truth”: not doing God’s commandments.

“But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another”. Then there is no fragmentation, no fermentation, no festering. “And the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin”: that is the atonement.

“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” We all have sin in us; we all have battles. You are saying, I’m good, I’m fine, I’m great, but you know that hatred for that brother or that sister is there. You are deceiving yourself.
“If we confess our sins”: confess our faults, which is Proverbs 28:13. “He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”

“If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar”: I don’t have to keep the law, I’m perfect, I’m righteous and holy, holier than thou. That makes God a liar. If you are perfect, with no sin at all, Christ died for no reason at all. “And his word is not in us.”
